cards.text: A business-school paper became a billion-dollar bet
cards.meaning: At Stanford, Knight wrote a paper arguing that Japanese running shoes could do to German brands what Japanese cameras had done. He called it his Crazy Idea and spent years proving it.
cards.apply: Write one page on the contrarian thesis you keep returning to, and list the cheapest test you could run this month.

cards.text: Cold-call the supplier before you have a company
cards.meaning: In 1962 he flew to Japan, met Onitsuka (maker of Tiger shoes) and invented the name Blue Ribbon on the spot to win US distribution rights. Nerve came before structure.
cards.apply: Reach out this week to one source, supplier or management team you have been waiting to feel ready for.

cards.text: Partner with someone obsessed with the product
cards.meaning: His old coach Bill Bowerman put in $500 to match Knight's and kept rebuilding shoes for his runners. The waffle-iron sole came from his kitchen experiments.
cards.apply: Find the person closest to your end user and ask what they would change about your product or report.

cards.text: Hire believers, then let them run
cards.meaning: First employee Jeff Johnson sent Knight long letters and opened stores with little direction. Knight learned that trusting odd, driven people beat micromanaging them.
cards.apply: Give one team member a problem with an outcome, not instructions, and stay out of the how.

cards.text: Fast growth can starve you of cash
cards.meaning: Sales doubled year after year, but every dollar went into inventory and the banks kept cutting his credit line. A profitable business still nearly died of illiquidity.
cards.apply: On any growth company you cover, compare working-capital build to operating cash flow before you trust the revenue story.

cards.text: Creative financing saved the company
cards.meaning: When banks walked away, the Japanese trading house Nissho Iwai extended credit against inventory. The right financing partner mattered as much as the right shoe.
cards.apply: Map who funds a company's working capital, and what happens if that source pulls back.

cards.text: Never let one supplier own your fate
cards.meaning: Onitsuka tried to replace Blue Ribbon with another distributor. The break forced Knight to launch his own brand, Nike, in 1972.
cards.apply: List your single points of failure (one client, one vendor, one data source) and start a backup for the biggest.

cards.text: A $35 logo and a borrowed goddess
cards.meaning: Student Carolyn Davidson designed the swoosh for $35, and Johnson suggested the name Nike, the Greek goddess of victory. Knight didn't love either at first; meaning came from the product.
cards.apply: Stop polishing the label on a project; ship it and let results give it weight.

cards.text: Athletes as the brand's soul
cards.meaning: Runners like Steve Prefontaine wore the shoes and carried the rebel spirit. His death in a 1975 car crash hit the company hard and deepened its sense of purpose.
cards.apply: Ask who embodies your work's best version, and learn what they need from you.

cards.text: A government bill nearly ended everything
cards.meaning: US Customs hit the company with a duty demand of about $25 million under an old valuation rule. Knight fought it politically and in court before settling.
cards.apply: Note the regulatory or tax tail risk in a thesis and size how bad a surprise bill would be.

cards.text: Going public was about survival, not glory
cards.meaning: Nike's 1980 IPO finally gave it the capital to stop living loan to loan. Knight resisted losing control and used two classes of shares to keep it.
cards.apply: When you read an S-1, check who keeps control after the float and why.

cards.text: Keep going; the race has no finish line
cards.meaning: Knight ends by admitting the costs, including time away from his family. Ambition worked, but it took a real toll.
cards.apply: Block one evening this week that work cannot touch.

cards.text: Cancer is ancient, not modern
cards.meaning: An Egyptian papyrus describing breast tumours notes that there was no treatment. Cancer looks newer only because people now live long enough to get it.
cards.apply: When a disease market grows, separate true rising incidence from ageing, screening and better diagnosis.

cards.text: Bigger surgery did not mean better outcomes
cards.meaning: William Halsted's radical mastectomy cut away ever more tissue on the theory that cancer spread outward. Later trials showed less mutilating surgery did about as well.
cards.apply: Ask for the controlled-trial evidence behind any 'more is better' treatment or strategy.

cards.text: Chemotherapy began with a long shot on child leukemia
cards.meaning: In the late 1940s Sidney Farber used aminopterin, a folate blocker, and briefly put children with leukemia into remission. It proved chemicals could push cancer back.
cards.apply: Look for the small proof-of-concept that opens a whole category, then ask who owns the follow-ons.

cards.text: Advocacy turned research into a national mission
cards.meaning: Mary Lasker and Farber lobbied Congress, helping produce the 1971 National Cancer Act. Money and politics shaped the science as much as labs did.
cards.apply: When modelling a biotech, track funding flows (NIH, policy, payers), not just pipeline data.

cards.text: Cures came from combinations, not single drugs
cards.meaning: Combining several drugs at once, as in MOPP for Hodgkin's lymphoma, achieved cures where one drug failed. Resistance had to be attacked from several sides.
cards.apply: Test any problem you're stuck on against two or three moves at once rather than one.

cards.text: Prevention beat treatment for lung cancer
cards.meaning: Studies by Doll and Hill and by Wynder and Graham around 1950 tied smoking to lung cancer. The 1964 US Surgeon General's report made it official, against fierce tobacco lobbying.
cards.apply: In consumer or healthcare work, flag products whose long-term liabilities are still being litigated.

cards.text: Screening helps only when it changes outcomes
cards.meaning: The Pap smear cut cervical cancer deaths, while some screening finds harmless tumours. Earlier detection is not automatically better.
cards.apply: Judge a diagnostics company by mortality or outcome data, not by how many cases it detects.

cards.text: Cancer is a disease of our own genes
cards.meaning: Work by Varmus and Bishop showed oncogenes are normal cellular genes gone wrong. That reframed cancer as broken growth controls inside our cells.
cards.apply: Read one plain-language review of the biology behind a drug you follow before your next model update.

cards.text: Targeted drugs hit the broken switch
cards.meaning: Herceptin targets HER2 in some breast cancers, and Gleevec blocks the BCR-ABL protein in chronic myeloid leukemia. Gleevec turned a fatal disease into a manageable one for many.
cards.apply: When valuing a targeted therapy, size the biomarker-positive population, not the whole disease.

cards.text: Cancer evolves to escape every weapon
cards.meaning: Like the Red Queen running to stay in place, tumours mutate and become resistant. Each victory tends to be partial.
cards.apply: Build resistance and durability assumptions into any oncology revenue forecast.

cards.text: Trials and patients, not heroes, move the field
cards.meaning: Mukherjee weaves in his own patients to show the human cost of each experiment. Progress came from thousands of trial volunteers.
cards.apply: When you read trial results, note the endpoints and the sample size before the headline.

cards.text: Progress is real but uneven
cards.meaning: Some cancers are now curable or chronic, while others barely budged. The book argues for steady, evidence-driven gains rather than a single cure.
cards.apply: Avoid pricing an oncology name on a 'cure' narrative; price the incremental benefit.

cards.text: A dream team built a hedge fund on models
cards.meaning: John Meriwether, from Salomon's arbitrage desk, launched Long-Term Capital Management in 1994. Partners included future Nobel laureates Myron Scholes and Robert Merton.
cards.apply: Credentials are not a risk control; ask what a strategy loses in its worst plausible month.

cards.text: Pick up nickels with lots of leverage
cards.meaning: LTCM bet that small price gaps between similar bonds would converge. Each trade earned little, so they borrowed heavily to make it pay.
cards.apply: For any levered return, divide by the leverage to see the raw edge underneath.

cards.text: Early returns bred dangerous confidence
cards.meaning: After fees, investors earned roughly 40% in each of the first two full years. Success made the partners and their lenders less cautious.
cards.apply: After a great run, re-underwrite your best position as if you were seeing it for the first time.

cards.text: Banks lent on reputation, not scrutiny
cards.meaning: Wall Street gave LTCM generous terms and little transparency because everyone wanted its business. Its derivatives positions ran to over a trillion dollars notional.
cards.apply: When a counterparty is too famous to question, ask the questions anyway.

cards.text: Returning capital raised the leverage
cards.meaning: At the end of 1997 LTCM handed back money to outside investors but kept its positions. Less equity meant even higher leverage.
cards.apply: Check whether a company's buyback or payout is funded by thinner equity rather than spare cash.

cards.text: Models assumed the past would repeat
cards.meaning: Risk estimates relied on historical volatility and correlations. Markets in 1998 moved in ways the history said were near impossible.
cards.apply: Stress-test portfolios with scenarios that have never happened, not just past ones.

cards.text: Russia's default triggered a flight to safety
cards.meaning: When Russia defaulted in August 1998, investors fled to the safest bonds. Spreads LTCM expected to narrow widened instead.
cards.apply: Identify which positions all depend on the same 'calm markets' assumption.

cards.text: In a crisis, correlations go to one
cards.meaning: Trades that looked unrelated all lost money together because every buyer wanted liquidity. Diversification vanished when it was needed most.
cards.apply: Group your holdings by what they need to go right, not by sector labels.

cards.text: Copycats make exits crowded
cards.meaning: Other firms ran similar trades and sold at the same time, deepening losses. Being right about value didn't matter if you were forced out first.
cards.apply: Estimate how crowded a trade is before you add, and how fast you could exit it.

cards.text: The Fed brokered a private rescue
cards.meaning: In September 1998 the New York Fed gathered banks that put in about $3.6 billion to take over LTCM. No public money was used, but the precedent mattered.
cards.apply: Note which institutions in a sector are systemically important enough to be rescued, and which aren't.

cards.text: Losses wiped out almost everything
cards.meaning: LTCM lost around $4.6 billion within months, and partners lost most of their own fortunes. The fund was wound down in 2000.
cards.apply: Size any single bet so that being wrong is painful but survivable.

cards.text: Markets can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent
cards.meaning: The line is widely attributed to Keynes, but no source in his writings has been found. LTCM lived its lesson either way: timing and funding kill good theses.
cards.apply: Match the funding horizon of each position to how long the thesis could take.

cards.text: Most 'strategies' are just goals in disguise
cards.meaning: Rumelt argues many corporate plans are lists of targets and slogans. A real strategy explains how you will overcome a specific obstacle.
cards.apply: Rewrite one of your goals as 'the obstacle is X, so we will do Y.'

cards.text: Fluff is a sign of bad strategy
cards.meaning: Buzzwords dress up the absence of thinking. If the language sounds impressive but says nothing, there's no strategy underneath.
cards.apply: Strip jargon from your next memo and see if the argument survives.

cards.text: Bad strategy refuses to name the problem
cards.meaning: If you can't state the key challenge, you can't choose how to tackle it. Avoiding the hard diagnosis is the most common failure.
cards.apply: Write the single sentence that names your team's biggest problem this quarter.

cards.text: The kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action
cards.meaning: Good strategy has three parts: a diagnosis of what's going on, a policy for dealing with it, and actions that reinforce each other.
cards.apply: Structure your next pitch or plan in those three headings.

cards.text: Strategy means choosing what not to do
cards.meaning: Saying yes to every stakeholder produces a wish list. Real strategy concentrates resources and disappoints someone.
cards.apply: Name one project you will drop or pause to fund your priority.

cards.text: Leverage comes from focus on a pivot point
cards.meaning: Advantage often comes from applying force at the one point where it matters most. Rumelt uses the 1991 Gulf War's flanking 'left hook' to illustrate.
cards.apply: Find the single variable that drives most of your thesis and spend your research hours there.

cards.text: Set proximate objectives you can actually hit
cards.meaning: A good objective is close enough to be feasible and clarifies the next move. Vague long-range aims paralyse teams.
cards.apply: Turn one big goal into a target your team can reach within 30 days.

cards.text: Jobs fixed Apple by cutting, not adding
cards.meaning: In 1997 Steve Jobs slashed Apple's product line down to a simple grid of four. Focus came before any new invention.
cards.apply: Audit your offerings or coverage list and cut the bottom quarter.

cards.text: Chain-link systems are only as good as their weakest link
cards.meaning: In some businesses, quality depends on every part working. Improving one strong link does nothing if another is weak.
cards.apply: Identify the weakest step in a process you own and fix it first.

cards.text: Ride the waves of change
cards.meaning: Big shifts in technology, cost or regulation reset advantages. Strategy means spotting the wave early and positioning before others.
cards.apply: List one structural change hitting your sector and who it helps or hurts.

cards.text: Growth is not a strategy
cards.meaning: Rumelt warns that growth for its own sake, often through deals, destroys value. Healthy growth is the result of advantage, not a goal.
cards.apply: When a company announces an acquisition, ask what advantage it extends.

cards.text: Think like a strategist: question your own first answer
cards.meaning: He suggests writing down your judgment and then critiquing it. Strategy improves when you argue against yourself.
cards.apply: Before finalising a recommendation, write the best case against it.

cards.text: A manager's output is the team's output
cards.meaning: Grove defines a manager's output as the output of their organisation plus the groups they influence. Your personal tasks count only through others.
cards.apply: List what your team shipped this week, not what you personally did.

cards.text: Run work like a breakfast factory
cards.meaning: He uses serving eggs, toast and coffee to explain production: find the limiting step and plan around it. Management is a production process.
cards.apply: Find the slowest step in a recurring workflow and schedule everything around it.

cards.text: Pair every indicator with its counter
cards.meaning: Measuring one thing causes people to game it, so pair it with a check. Track output alongside quality.
cards.apply: Add a quality metric to any speed or volume metric you track.

cards.text: Leverage is the heart of management
cards.meaning: Some activities affect many people, like a good decision or training. Pick tasks with the highest leverage.
cards.apply: Spend one hour this week on an activity that multiplies others' work, such as a template or training.

cards.text: One-on-ones belong to the report
cards.meaning: Grove's one-on-ones are the subordinate's meeting, with their agenda. They surface problems early and teach.
cards.apply: Schedule a one-on-one and ask the other person to bring the agenda.

cards.text: Meetings are a manager's medium
cards.meaning: Process meetings keep the routine running; mission meetings solve one problem. Each needs a clear purpose.
cards.apply: Cancel or redefine one meeting that lacks a clear outcome.

cards.text: Decisions need free discussion, then clear commitment
cards.meaning: Grove describes debate, a clear decision, then full support. Peer-level decisions often stall without it.
cards.apply: For your next decision, set a deadline and announce who decides.

cards.text: Planning is about today's actions
cards.meaning: Planning means deciding what to do now to shape the future. Outputs without today's moves are wishful thinking.
cards.apply: Translate one annual goal into this week's concrete action.

cards.text: Objectives and key results keep focus
cards.meaning: Intel used objectives with measurable key results, which later spread as OKRs. Key results should be checkable.
cards.apply: Write one objective with two measurable key results for next month.

cards.text: Match your style to task-relevant maturity
cards.meaning: Inexperienced people need structure; experienced ones need autonomy. Style depends on the person and the task.
cards.apply: Adjust how closely you supervise one person based on their experience with the task.

cards.text: Training is the manager's job
cards.meaning: Grove argues training is among the highest-leverage things a manager can do. Don't outsource it.
cards.apply: Teach your team one skill you know well this week.

cards.text: Performance reviews are for improving, not judging
cards.meaning: Reviews should give specific, honest feedback to raise performance. Vague praise wastes the opportunity.
cards.apply: Give one colleague specific feedback on a recent piece of work.

cards.text: Science is a candle in the dark
cards.meaning: Sagan's subtitle frames science as a fragile light against superstition. It's a way of thinking, not just a body of facts.
cards.apply: Pick one belief you hold and ask what evidence would change your mind.

cards.text: Pair openness with tough scepticism
cards.meaning: He argues for wonder and rigour together. Too much openness believes anything; too much scepticism learns nothing.
cards.apply: Approach one new claim this week with curiosity first, then check the evidence.

cards.text: Carry a baloney detection kit
cards.meaning: Sagan lists tools: seek independent confirmation, encourage debate, discount authority, and spin multiple hypotheses.
cards.apply: Run your next investment thesis through that checklist before presenting it.

cards.text: Beware common fallacies
cards.meaning: The kit also names traps: ad hominem, appeal to authority, small numbers, confusing correlation with causation.
cards.apply: Find one fallacy in a recent article or pitch and note how you'd correct it.

cards.text: The invisible dragon in the garage
cards.meaning: Sagan imagines a dragon that can't be seen, heard or detected. A claim that can't be tested is no different from no claim.
cards.apply: Ask of any forecast: what result would prove it wrong?

cards.text: Extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence
cards.meaning: Sagan popularised this line in Cosmos (1980); similar ideas go back to Laplace and Marcello Truzzi. The bigger the claim, the stronger the proof needed.
cards.apply: Raise your evidence bar for the boldest assumption in your model.

cards.text: Memory and perception can deceive us
cards.meaning: Sagan explores alien-abduction stories and how sincere people recall things that didn't happen. Honesty isn't proof.
cards.apply: Verify a key fact from an interview with an independent source.

cards.text: Patterns appear where none exist
cards.meaning: The 'Face on Mars' was a trick of light and shadow, later clarified by better images. Our brains find faces and patterns everywhere.
cards.apply: Before trusting a chart pattern, test it on more data.

cards.text: Science corrects its own errors
cards.meaning: Science's strength is that it admits mistakes and updates. Authority yields to evidence.
cards.apply: Note one view you have updated recently and why.

cards.text: Witch hunts show the cost of abandoning evidence
cards.meaning: Sagan describes witch trials where accusation became proof. Fear without evidence destroys lives.
cards.apply: Ask for evidence before acting on a rumour about a colleague or company.

cards.text: A tech society needs science literacy
cards.meaning: He worried about a society relying on technology few understand. Ignorance leaves people vulnerable to charlatans.
cards.apply: Learn the basics of one technology central to your work.

cards.text: Teach curiosity, not just answers
cards.meaning: Sagan wants schools to teach how to ask questions and weigh evidence. Children are natural scientists.
cards.apply: Ask 'how do we know?' in your next team discussion.

title: Genghis Khan and the Making of the Modern World
author: Jack Weatherford

cards.text: Born into hardship on the steppe
cards.meaning: Temujin, born around 1162, lost his father Yesugei to poisoning and was abandoned by his clan with his family. Survival shaped his ruthlessness.
cards.apply: Reflect on one setback that strengthened you, and how it can inform your next challenge.

cards.text: Loyalty over bloodline
cards.meaning: Temujin built alliances based on loyalty rather than kinship. Followers rose on merit.
cards.apply: Recognise one colleague's contribution regardless of their title.

cards.text: Rescuing Börte built his coalition
cards.meaning: When Merkits kidnapped his wife Börte, he allied with Toghrul and Jamuka to rescue her. The raid proved his ability to lead others.
cards.apply: Ask a peer for help on a goal you can't achieve alone.

cards.text: He became Genghis Khan in 1206
cards.meaning: A great gathering proclaimed him ruler of the steppe tribes. Unity replaced constant feuding.
cards.apply: Bring a divided group together around one shared objective.

cards.text: Decimal units broke tribal loyalties
cards.meaning: He organised his army in units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000, mixing tribes. Loyalty went to the unit and the khan.
cards.apply: Mix teams across silos to break down old divisions.

cards.text: Promotion by merit
cards.meaning: Commanders rose based on performance, not aristocratic birth. That gave talent room to grow.
cards.apply: Give a junior person a stretch assignment based on ability.

cards.text: Law above the leader
cards.meaning: The Mongol law, the Yassa, set rules for conduct. Weatherford argues even the khan was bound by it.
cards.apply: Write down the rules of your team so everyone follows them, including you.

cards.text: Religious tolerance kept the empire together
cards.meaning: The Mongols allowed many faiths and exempted clergy from some taxes. Tolerance reduced resistance.
cards.apply: Welcome different perspectives in your next team discussion.

cards.text: Speed and information won battles
cards.meaning: Mobile cavalry and the yam relay system carried messages quickly across the empire. Information moved faster than enemies could react.
cards.apply: Shorten one feedback loop in your work this week.

cards.text: He absorbed the skills of the conquered
cards.meaning: The Mongols recruited engineers, doctors and craftsmen from conquered peoples. Siege warfare came from Chinese and Persian experts.
cards.apply: Learn one skill from a colleague in a different field.

cards.text: Insult brought catastrophe on Khwarazm
cards.meaning: When the Khwarazmian empire killed Mongol envoys and traders around 1219, Genghis Khan destroyed it. Violence was terrifying and deliberate.
cards.apply: Treat partners with respect; broken trust can be costly.

cards.text: Trade and connection outlived conquest
cards.meaning: Weatherford argues the Mongol empire linked East and West, spreading trade, ideas and technology. He died in 1227, but the networks endured.
cards.apply: Look for the lasting networks behind any short-term win.

cards.text: Written in days, after years in the camps
cards.meaning: Frankl, a Viennese psychiatrist, survived Auschwitz and Dachau and wrote the book in 1946. It records what helped people endure.
cards.apply: Write down what keeps you going when work gets hard.

cards.text: Shock, apathy, then a strange release
cards.meaning: He describes three phases of prisoners' experience: admission, camp life and liberation. Even freedom brought numbness and bitterness.
cards.apply: Notice which phase you're in during a major change and be patient with it.

cards.text: Love sustained him
cards.meaning: Thinking of his wife, not knowing whether she lived, gave him strength. Inner life could survive outer misery.
cards.apply: Spend focused time with someone who matters to you this week.

cards.text: The last freedom is choosing your attitude
cards.meaning: Frankl argues that circumstances can take everything except how you respond. That choice gives dignity.
cards.apply: Choose your response to one frustrating situation before reacting.

cards.text: Those who lost hope often died
cards.meaning: He saw prisoners give up when they lost faith in the future. Hope was a matter of survival.
cards.apply: Set one meaningful goal for the coming months.

cards.text: A why helps you bear almost any how
cards.meaning: Frankl quotes this idea from Nietzsche. Purpose makes suffering bearable.
cards.apply: Write down the 'why' behind your current project.

cards.text: Meaning comes from three sources
cards.meaning: Logotherapy names creating a work or deed, experiencing love, and the attitude we take to unavoidable suffering.
cards.apply: Pick one way to add meaning this week: a task, a relationship, or a hard situation you face well.

cards.text: The will to meaning drives us
cards.meaning: Frankl contrasts Freud's pleasure and Adler's power with the human need for meaning. Lack of meaning leads to an 'existential vacuum'.
cards.apply: Ask whether your current goals give you meaning or just distraction.

cards.text: Life asks us questions
cards.meaning: Rather than asking what we expect from life, Frankl says life expects something of us. Responsibility answers.
cards.apply: Ask what your situation requires of you today.

cards.text: A Statue of Responsibility
cards.meaning: He suggested the Statue of Liberty on the East Coast be balanced by one of Responsibility on the West. Freedom needs accountability.
cards.apply: Take ownership of one problem you've been avoiding.

cards.text: Tragic optimism
cards.meaning: In a later postscript, Frankl describes staying hopeful despite pain, guilt and death. Optimism is a choice, not denial.
cards.apply: Find one lesson in a recent setback.

cards.text: The 'space between stimulus and response' isn't his
cards.meaning: The quote is widely attributed to Frankl, but its source is unclear and it hasn't been found in his writings. The idea is still close to his thinking.
cards.apply: Pause for a breath before responding to a stressful message.

cards.text: The most powerful man in New York was never elected
cards.meaning: Robert Moses shaped New York's roads, bridges, parks and housing for about four decades. His only run for office, for governor in 1934, ended in a heavy defeat.
cards.apply: When you analyse a city or development market, find out who actually controls approvals and capital, not just who holds office.

cards.text: He started as a reformer, not a fixer
cards.meaning: The young Moses was an idealistic civil-service reformer whose plans were ignored. He learned that good ideas without power changed nothing.
cards.apply: Pair your next proposal with a clear answer to who has to say yes and why they would.

cards.text: He wrote the laws that gave him power
cards.meaning: Moses drafted bills himself, burying broad powers in dense legal language that legislators passed without reading closely. Control often hides in the fine print.
cards.apply: Read the governing documents of one deal you're on (covenants, bylaws, permits) for clauses that shift control.

cards.text: Jones Beach proved he could deliver
cards.meaning: His state parks and Jones Beach on Long Island won him huge public popularity. That reputation for getting things built shielded him for decades.
cards.apply: Build credibility with one visible, on-time delivery before asking for bigger mandates.

cards.text: Toll revenue was his real power base
cards.meaning: Through public authorities like the Triborough Bridge Authority, Moses controlled toll income and issued bonds against it. That money let him fund projects without asking politicians.
cards.apply: When valuing infrastructure or real assets, trace who controls the cash flows and the debt they support.

cards.text: Bond covenants made him almost untouchable
cards.meaning: The authority's bond contracts made his position hard to remove without upsetting bondholders. Investors became his shield.
cards.apply: Check how financing terms constrain management or owners before assuming a change of strategy is possible.

cards.text: He held many titles at once
cards.meaning: At his peak Moses held a dozen city and state posts at the same time. Overlapping roles let him coordinate everything and answer to no one.
cards.apply: Map concentration of decision-making in a company you cover; key-person risk is real.

cards.text: Highways bred more traffic
cards.meaning: Caro shows that new expressways filled up quickly, as more people chose to drive. Building roads didn't solve congestion.
cards.apply: Stress-test demand assumptions for any project that may create the very usage it plans to serve.

cards.text: Transit lost out to the car
cards.meaning: Moses favoured roads and bridges over rail and mass transit. Caro argues that choice shaped decades of sprawl and congestion.
cards.apply: When underwriting a location, weigh transit access alongside road links.

cards.text: One mile of the Cross-Bronx Expressway
cards.meaning: Caro describes how Moses pushed the expressway through the East Tremont neighbourhood, displacing many families when alternative routes existed. The human cost was ignored.
cards.apply: Include displacement and community impact in your assessment of any big development.

cards.text: Power corrupts the original vision
cards.meaning: Over time Moses became more arrogant and less responsive to public need. Caro's theme is how power changed him.
cards.apply: Ask for honest feedback on a project you champion, especially from those affected.

cards.text: He finally fell when the money moved
cards.meaning: In 1968 Governor Nelson Rockefeller folded the Triborough Authority into the new MTA, ending Moses's control. Whoever takes the purse takes the power.
cards.apply: Watch for structural shifts in funding, since they often precede leadership change.

cards.text: Boeing was once an engineers' company
cards.meaning: For decades Boeing was known for engineering-led culture and bold bets like the 747. Safety and quality defined the brand.
cards.apply: Ask what a company's culture prized during its best years, and whether that's still true.

cards.text: The McDonnell Douglas merger changed the culture
cards.meaning: After the 1997 merger, executives from McDonnell Douglas, including Harry Stonecipher, pushed a sharper focus on costs and shareholder returns. Robison sees this as the turning point.
cards.apply: After a merger, track which company's leaders end up running the combined firm.

cards.text: Headquarters moved away from the factory
cards.meaning: In 2001 Boeing moved its head office from Seattle to Chicago, far from its engineers. Distance weakened the link between leaders and the product.
cards.apply: Spend time where the product is made or the service delivered before forming a view on management.

cards.text: Airbus forced a rushed response
cards.meaning: When Airbus's fuel-efficient A320neo won major orders, including from American Airlines in 2011, Boeing chose to update the 737 rather than design a new plane. Speed and cost won.
cards.apply: When a competitor forces a response, compare the cost of a quick fix with the long-term risk.

cards.text: Bigger engines changed how the plane handled
cards.meaning: The MAX's larger engines were mounted further forward and higher, which could push the nose up in some conditions. Software was added to compensate.
cards.apply: Ask how a product's core design was modified to fit a new requirement, and what that introduced.

cards.text: MCAS relied on a single sensor
cards.meaning: The flight-control software MCAS took input from one angle-of-attack sensor. A faulty reading could push the nose down repeatedly.
cards.apply: Identify single points of failure in any system you depend on.

cards.text: Pilots weren't told about the system
cards.meaning: To avoid costly simulator training, Boeing pitched the MAX as similar to older 737s, and MCAS was left out of pilot manuals. Saving airline training costs was a selling point.
cards.apply: Check whether a company's sales promise depends on downplaying a risk.

cards.text: Two crashes killed 346 people
cards.meaning: Lion Air Flight 610 crashed in October 2018 and Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302 in March 2019. Both involved MCAS activating on faulty data.
cards.apply: Treat a first incident as a warning signal, not an anomaly, in any risk you track.

cards.text: Regulators relied on Boeing to certify itself
cards.meaning: The FAA had delegated much certification work to Boeing employees. Oversight weakened when the regulator lacked resources.
cards.apply: Assess how independent oversight actually is in a regulated sector you follow.

cards.text: The fleet was grounded worldwide
cards.meaning: The MAX was grounded globally in March 2019 for about 20 months. Costs, compensation and lost orders ran into billions.
cards.apply: Model a grounding or recall scenario for any manufacturer with concentrated product risk.

cards.text: Buybacks competed with investment
cards.meaning: Robison notes Boeing spent heavily on share repurchases in the years before the crisis. Capital went to shareholders rather than new designs.
cards.apply: Compare buybacks with R&D and capex over five years when evaluating a capital-intensive firm.

cards.text: Leadership paid the price, late
cards.meaning: CEO Dennis Muilenburg was ousted in December 2019 after the crisis deepened. Accountability came only after the damage was done.
cards.apply: Watch how management responds to the first bad news; it predicts the rest.

cards.text: Six materials hold up the modern world
cards.meaning: Conway follows sand, salt, iron, copper, oil and lithium. Behind every digital product sits an enormous physical supply chain.
cards.apply: List the physical inputs behind one company you cover, even a software one.

cards.text: We dig more than ever
cards.meaning: Despite talk of a weightless economy, humanity extracts more material each year than before. Growth still needs mining.
cards.apply: Question any thesis that assumes demand for raw materials is shrinking.

cards.text: Sand becomes glass, concrete and chips
cards.meaning: Sand is turned into concrete, glass and the silicon at the heart of computing. Not all sand is equal.
cards.apply: Look for niche grades or specs that make a 'commodity' scarce.

cards.text: Ultra-pure quartz is a chokepoint
cards.meaning: High-purity quartz from Spruce Pine, North Carolina, is critical for making the crucibles used to grow silicon crystals. A few small places matter globally.
cards.apply: Identify single-source suppliers in a value chain you analyse.

cards.text: Chips depend on extreme purification
cards.meaning: Turning silicon into chips requires purity and precision few industries match. Each step adds value and concentration.
cards.apply: Map where value and margins accumulate along the chain from raw material to product.

cards.text: Salt feeds the chemical industry
cards.meaning: Salt is a feedstock for chlorine and caustic soda, used in water treatment, plastics and more. It's far more than seasoning.
cards.apply: Trace one ordinary input to the industries it supports.

cards.text: Steel is the backbone, and hard to clean
cards.meaning: Iron ore and coking coal make most steel, a big source of emissions. Greener methods are possible but costly.
cards.apply: When analysing steel or construction names, track the cost of decarbonisation.

cards.text: Copper wires the energy transition
cards.meaning: Electrification, from grids to electric cars, needs vast amounts of copper. Ore grades at many mines are falling.
cards.apply: Check reserve life and grade trends before valuing a copper miner.

cards.text: Oil is also plastic and chemicals
cards.meaning: Oil isn't just fuel; it makes plastics and chemicals used everywhere. The transition away from it is complicated.
cards.apply: Split an oil company's exposure between fuel and petrochemicals.

cards.text: Lithium powers batteries
cards.meaning: Lithium comes from brines in South America and hard rock in Australia. Refining is heavily concentrated in China.
cards.apply: Assess geopolitical concentration risk in battery supply chains.

cards.text: Supply chains are fragile and global
cards.meaning: Conway shows how a few countries and companies dominate key steps. Disruption in one place spreads.
cards.apply: Ask management about contingency plans for a single-country supply risk.

cards.text: The physical economy deserves attention
cards.meaning: His message is that we've forgotten how much depends on mining and processing. Investors ignore it at their peril.
cards.apply: Read one mining or materials report this week to understand the physical side.

cards.text: Four central bankers ran the world economy
cards.meaning: Ahamed follows Montagu Norman of the Bank of England, Benjamin Strong of the New York Fed, Hjalmar Schacht of the Reichsbank and Émile Moreau of the Banque de France. Their choices shaped the 1920s and the Depression.
cards.apply: Read one recent speech from a central bank governor that affects your portfolio.

cards.text: War debts and reparations poisoned the system
cards.meaning: After World War I, Germany owed reparations and Allies owed the US war debts. These obligations strained the whole system.
cards.apply: Map who owes whom in any macro scenario you analyse.

cards.text: Germany's hyperinflation scarred a nation
cards.meaning: In 1923 German prices exploded and savings were wiped out. Schacht helped stabilise the currency with the Rentenmark.
cards.apply: Consider how past inflation shapes a country's policy choices today.

cards.text: Britain returned to gold at the old rate
cards.meaning: In 1925 Britain went back to the gold standard at its pre-war parity, with Churchill as Chancellor. Keynes argued the pound was overvalued.
cards.apply: Test whether a currency peg or policy target is set at a realistic level.

cards.text: Overvalued money hurt Britain's economy
cards.meaning: The strong pound made exports expensive and kept unemployment high. Defending the peg meant tight policy.
cards.apply: Note how currency strength affects exporters in your coverage.

cards.text: France piled up gold
cards.meaning: An undervalued franc after 1926 drew gold to France. Gold accumulating in a few places tightened conditions elsewhere.
cards.apply: Watch reserve flows between major economies.

cards.text: A 1927 rate cut may have fed the boom
cards.meaning: Strong eased US policy in 1927 partly to support sterling. Critics argue this added fuel to the stock market bubble.
cards.apply: Ask how international pressures are influencing your own central bank's choices.

cards.text: Leadership gaps mattered
cards.meaning: Strong died in 1928, leaving the Fed without a forceful leader as the crisis came. Institutions depend on people.
cards.apply: Note key-person risk at the institutions you rely on.

cards.text: The crash turned into a global depression
cards.meaning: After 1929, falling prices, bank failures and gold-standard rigidity spread the collapse worldwide. Austria's Creditanstalt failed in 1931.
cards.apply: Look for contagion channels, such as bank links, in a stressed market.

cards.text: The gold standard was a straitjacket
cards.meaning: Ahamed argues that tying currencies to gold forced countries to tighten when they needed to ease. Rules meant to bring stability deepened the slump.
cards.apply: Question whether a rigid policy rule is hurting more than helping.

cards.text: Leaving gold early helped recovery
cards.meaning: Britain left gold in 1931 and the US effectively in 1933; countries that left earlier tended to recover sooner.
cards.apply: In crises, look for policy flexibility as a signal of earlier recovery.

cards.text: Ideas and personalities shape markets
cards.meaning: The book shows how beliefs and egos, not just data, drove decisions. Understanding policymakers matters.
cards.apply: Study the background and views of the policymaker most relevant to your work.

cards.text: A golden age of science in Arabic
cards.meaning: Al-Khalili argues that for centuries, much of the world's best science was written in Arabic. Scholars came from many faiths and backgrounds.
cards.apply: Seek out one idea from a tradition you rarely read.

cards.text: Baghdad's translation movement
cards.meaning: Under the Abbasids, scholars translated Greek, Persian and Indian works into Arabic. Caliph al-Ma'mun (r. 813–833) was a major patron.
cards.apply: Learn from the best existing work before trying to build something new.

cards.text: The House of Wisdom
cards.meaning: The Bayt al-Hikma in Baghdad became a symbol of this learning. Al-Khalili notes historians debate its exact role.
cards.apply: Create a space, even a folder, to collect the best thinking in your field.

cards.text: Paper spread knowledge
cards.meaning: Paper-making, learned from China, spread through the Islamic world from the 8th century. Cheaper writing material helped ideas spread.
cards.apply: Look for the cheap technology that makes a new wave of ideas possible.

cards.text: Al-Khwarizmi gave us algebra
cards.meaning: His book on 'al-jabr' gave its name to algebra, and his name gave us 'algorithm'. He also helped spread Indian numerals.
cards.apply: Break a complex problem into standard steps you can repeat.

cards.text: Al-Razi observed patients carefully
cards.meaning: Al-Razi distinguished smallpox from measles based on clinical observation. Medicine advanced through careful records.
cards.apply: Keep notes on outcomes to learn what works in your own decisions.

cards.text: Ibn al-Haytham insisted on experiment
cards.meaning: His Book of Optics argued light enters the eye and tested ideas through experiment. Al-Khalili calls him a pioneer of scientific method.
cards.apply: Test an assumption with a small experiment before acting on it.

cards.text: Al-Biruni measured the Earth
cards.meaning: Al-Biruni estimated the Earth's radius using mountain observations. He combined mathematics with careful measurement.
cards.apply: Use simple measurement to check a big claim.

cards.text: Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine
cards.meaning: Ibn Sina (Avicenna) wrote the Canon, used in Europe for centuries. It organised medical knowledge systematically.
cards.apply: Summarise the core knowledge of your field in one organised document.

cards.text: Maragha observatory and al-Tusi
cards.meaning: Nasir al-Din al-Tusi worked at the Maragha observatory and devised the 'Tusi couple'. Similar geometry later appears in Copernicus.
cards.apply: Notice how ideas travel between cultures and centuries.

cards.text: Why did the golden age fade?
cards.meaning: Al-Khalili argues the decline had many causes, including political turmoil and economics. He rejects blaming one thinker, such as al-Ghazali, alone.
cards.apply: Look for multiple causes when explaining any decline.

cards.text: Science is a shared human inheritance
cards.meaning: The book argues modern science draws on many civilisations. Recognising that history matters.
cards.apply: Credit the sources of ideas you use in your work.

cards.text: The story starts in 63 BCE
cards.meaning: Beard opens with Cicero exposing Catiline's alleged conspiracy. It shows Roman politics, rhetoric and the question of citizens' rights.
cards.apply: Look at a key moment to understand a larger system.

cards.text: Rome's founding myths were troubling
cards.meaning: Romulus killed Remus, and Rome was said to welcome outsiders and refugees. Romans told stories about fratricide and openness.
cards.apply: Examine the stories your organisation tells about itself.

cards.text: Early history is mostly myth
cards.meaning: Beard separates legends of kings from limited evidence. Historians must admit what they don't know.
cards.apply: Distinguish clearly between facts and narratives in your analysis.

cards.text: The Republic balanced power
cards.meaning: Annual magistrates, the Senate and the people's assemblies shared power. No one person was supposed to dominate.
cards.apply: Build checks into how decisions are made in your team.

cards.text: Rome grew by alliances
cards.meaning: Rome expanded by making conquered peoples allies who supplied soldiers. Manpower drove further expansion.
cards.apply: Look for partnerships that multiply resources.

cards.text: Citizenship was Rome's secret
cards.meaning: Rome extended citizenship to outsiders, especially after the Social War of 91–88 BCE. Inclusion strengthened loyalty.
cards.apply: Bring outsiders into your network as real partners.

cards.text: Violence broke the Republic
cards.meaning: From the Gracchi onward, political violence grew. Norms eroded before institutions collapsed.
cards.apply: Watch for erosion of norms as a warning sign in any institution.

cards.text: Caesar and Augustus ended the Republic
cards.meaning: Caesar's dictatorship and Augustus's rule turned Rome into one-man government. Augustus kept republican forms while holding power.
cards.apply: Notice when form and substance diverge in governance.

cards.text: Emperors mattered less than you think
cards.meaning: Beard argues the system worked similarly regardless of which emperor ruled. Structure mattered more than personality.
cards.apply: Focus on systems, not just leaders, when evaluating organisations.

cards.text: Ordinary Romans had lives too
cards.meaning: Beard uses graffiti, bars and tombstones to show daily life. History isn't only about elites.
cards.apply: Talk to frontline staff to understand how your company works.

cards.text: Citizenship for all free people in 212 CE
cards.meaning: Caracalla granted citizenship to nearly all free inhabitants of the empire. Beard ends her story there.
cards.apply: Consider how broadening access can transform a system.

cards.text: Rome still shapes debates
cards.meaning: Beard argues Rome helps us think about citizenship, power and freedom today. History is a conversation.
cards.apply: Use a historical example in your next strategic discussion.

cards.text: What blocks you can become the path
cards.meaning: Holiday builds on a passage in Marcus Aurelius's Meditations: the impediment to action can advance action. Obstacles become opportunities.
cards.apply: Pick one obstacle and ask how it could help you.

cards.text: Three disciplines: perception, action, will
cards.meaning: Holiday organises the book around how we see problems, what we do, and how we endure.
cards.apply: Use those three as a checklist for a problem you face.

cards.text: Control your perceptions
cards.meaning: How you see a situation shapes your response. Strip away emotion to see clearly.
cards.apply: Write a neutral description of a problem before reacting.

cards.text: Rockefeller stayed calm in panics
cards.meaning: Holiday describes John D. Rockefeller's composure from the Panic of 1857 onward. Calm let him see opportunity.
cards.apply: Treat market drawdowns as a time for clear thinking, not panic.

cards.text: Focus on what you control
cards.meaning: Stoics separate what's in our control from what isn't. Energy should go to the former.
cards.apply: List what you control in a stressful situation and act on it.

cards.text: Act, and keep acting
cards.meaning: Holiday stresses persistence and iteration. Progress comes from steady action.
cards.apply: Take one small step today on a stalled project.

cards.text: Grant kept trying at Vicksburg
cards.meaning: Ulysses S. Grant tried several approaches before taking Vicksburg in 1863. Persistence won.
cards.apply: Try a different approach to a problem rather than giving up.

cards.text: Demosthenes trained to overcome weakness
cards.meaning: The Greek orator worked hard to overcome speech difficulties. Training can turn weakness into strength.
cards.apply: Practise a weak skill deliberately this week.

cards.text: Prepare for what could go wrong
cards.meaning: The Stoic premeditatio malorum means imagining setbacks in advance. Preparation reduces fear.
cards.apply: Do a pre-mortem on your next big decision.

cards.text: Edison's fire
cards.meaning: Holiday recounts Thomas Edison's response to the 1914 fire at his laboratory complex: he started rebuilding quickly.
cards.apply: After a setback, plan your first rebuilding step immediately.

cards.text: Love your fate
cards.meaning: Amor fati means accepting and even embracing what happens. It frees energy for action.
cards.apply: Find one thing to appreciate in a recent setback.

cards.text: Every obstacle is a chance to practise virtue
cards.meaning: Holiday argues obstacles are chances for courage, patience and creativity. Life will keep testing us.
cards.apply: Choose a virtue to practise in the next difficult moment.

cards.text: Experts often forecast poorly
cards.meaning: Tetlock's earlier research found many expert predictions were barely better than chance. He joked about a dart-throwing chimp.
cards.apply: Track the accuracy of forecasts you rely on.

cards.text: Foxes beat hedgehogs
cards.meaning: Forecasters who drew on many ideas (foxes) did better than those with one big theory (hedgehogs). Flexibility helps.
cards.apply: Consider several frameworks before making a call.

cards.text: Forecasting can be measured
cards.meaning: Tetlock uses Brier scores to measure accuracy. Without scoring, no one learns.
cards.apply: Write down a probability for one forecast and score it later.

cards.text: The Good Judgment Project won a tournament
cards.meaning: In a US intelligence-funded forecasting tournament, Tetlock's volunteers outperformed rivals. Some beat analysts with access to classified data.
cards.apply: Test whether well-trained amateurs could match experts in your field.

cards.text: Superforecasters are made, not born
cards.meaning: The best forecasters weren't geniuses; they had habits of careful thinking. Training improved results.
cards.apply: Adopt one forecasting habit, such as base rates, this week.

cards.text: Break big questions into small ones
cards.meaning: Like Enrico Fermi, superforecasters split hard questions into estimable parts.
cards.apply: Decompose a forecast into its key drivers.

cards.text: Start with the outside view
cards.meaning: Begin with base rates from similar cases, then adjust for specifics. People often start with the inside view.
cards.apply: Find the base rate before forming your view.

cards.text: Update often in small steps
cards.meaning: Superforecasters revise forecasts as news arrives, usually incrementally.
cards.apply: Revisit a forecast after new information and adjust modestly.

cards.text: Granularity matters
cards.meaning: Distinguishing between 60% and 65% improves accuracy. Vague words like 'likely' hide meaning.
cards.apply: Use numbers instead of vague words in your next forecast.

cards.text: Teams can forecast better
cards.meaning: Well-run teams that challenge each other improved accuracy. Groupthink must be avoided.
cards.apply: Ask a colleague to challenge your forecast.

cards.text: Perpetual beta
cards.meaning: Superforecasters treat their views as works in progress and learn from mistakes.
cards.apply: Review one wrong forecast to learn why.

cards.text: Leaders need humility and decisiveness
cards.meaning: Tetlock discusses balancing confidence with openness. Leaders must act despite uncertainty.
cards.apply: Make a decision with a clear probability and a plan to revisit it.
